title: This study looks at how and with whom connected cars share your data
gist: A Northeastern University and Consumer Reports study measuring network traffic from 21 connected cars across 19 brands found widespread sharing with advertisers, trackers and Big Tech, led by Tesla's Model 3 contacting 34 ad/tracking/analytics domains, with companion apps adding more; automakers largely deflected responsibility, though Honda changed practices.

insights.claim: Testing 21 cars from 19 brands, Northeastern University and Consumer Reports researchers found traffic to advertisers, trackers and Big Tech firms like Microsoft and Adobe.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Automaker data monetization practices face growing privacy and regulatory scrutiny.
insights.locator: In news that should surprise very few

insights.claim: Tesla's Model 3 contacted the most third-party domains: 34 advertising, tracking and analytics domains plus 37 from integrated infotainment apps, while the Buick Envista and Mercedes-Benz EQS contacted only first-party domains.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Wide variation shows data sharing is a design choice, with reputational risk for heavy sharers.
insights.locator: All of the cars contacted a first-party domain

insights.claim: Alphabet domains were most frequently contacted due to Android Automotive OS, including advertising domains like doubleclick.net and googlesyndication.com not needed for core services.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Android Automotive gives Google an advertising data foothold inside cars.
insights.quote: But many of the [second-level domains] we observed were not necessary for core services
insights.locator: Alphabet’s domains were the most frequently

insights.claim: Using infotainment caused cars to contact the most domains, except the Tesla Cybertruck, which contacted 26 more third-party domains while driving than stationary.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Driving-time data collection is a material privacy exposure.
insights.locator: Using a car’s infotainment system resulted

insights.claim: Testing 30 connected car apps showed some expose users to more than 20 new advertising, tracking and analytics companies, with General Motors, Toyota and Nissan the worst offenders.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Companion apps multiply privacy risk and potential liability for these automakers.
insights.locator: Next, they tested 30 different connected car apps

insights.claim: In a Faraday tent, some EVs including Cadillac Lyriq, Chevrolet Blazer, Honda Prologue and Rivian R1S stopped connected subsystems without cellular, while others redirected traffic to Wi-Fi.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Fallback behaviors reveal data flows that persist even without cellular links.

insights.claim: Of 17 automakers contacted, 14 responded, all saying third-party sharing is covered by contracts prohibiting PII use beyond their privacy agreements, while seven said consumers are responsible for reading terms.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Industry relies on contractual and consent defenses that regulators may find inadequate.

insights.claim: Declining data-sharing agreements can cost users services and functionality they expected when buying the car.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Coercive consent design may attract consumer-protection enforcement.
insights.locator: Some of the automakers also deflected

insights.claim: After being contacted, Honda stopped sharing precise location data with at least one tracking company.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Shows public scrutiny can change automaker data practices.
insights.locator: However, there was at least one positive

insights.claim: The Mozilla Foundation's 2023 review of automaker privacy policies called cars the worst product category it had ever reviewed for privacy.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Persistent privacy failures across years increase regulatory risk for the auto sector.
insights.quote: “cars are the worst product category we have ever reviewed for privacy.”
